dataset.name: Root biomass and traits across four lowland Panamanian forests from 0 - 1.2 m soil depths
description: Fine roots are key to ecosystem-scale nutrient, carbon (C), and water cycling, yet our understanding of fine root traits variation within and among tropical forests, one of Earth’s most C-rich ecosystems, is limited. We characterized root biomass, morphology, nutrient content, and arbuscular mycorrhizal fungal (AMF) colonization in 10 cm increments to 1.2 m depth across four distinct lowland Panamanian forests.

The datasets provided include a .xlsx file for fine root characteristics across 10 cm increment depths to 1.2 m collected from late 2017 to 2018 across four different forests. Root characteristics include live fine root biomass, dead fine root biomass, coarse root biomass, specific root length, root diameter, root tissue density, specific root area, arbuscular mycorrhizal fungi colonization, root chemistry (e.g., organic chemistry), root %N, root %C, root C/N ratio, and root radiocarbon content. This .xlsx file contain four tabs with 1) Dataset; 2) Metadata with information about each column in the dataset; 3) The sampling methods summarized; 4) Sites information. We also provided csv files for each of these tabs. Additionally, a .kml file is provided with coordinates for all 32 plots included in the study across four forests (n = 8 plots per site/forest). This dataset serves as baseline data before a throughfall exclusion experiment, Panama Rainforest Changes with Experimental Drying (PARCHED), was implemented. No special software is needed to open these files.

Study Sites & Design:
This study was conducted in four distinct lowland seasonal tropical forests located across gradients in rainfall and soil fertility on the Isthmus of Panama. The sites are a subset of a larger network of ~50 1-ha long-term plots maintained by the Smithsonian Tropical Research Institute (STRI) in the Panamanian lowlands. The four forests span an increase of 1,000 mm MAP, and include three forests on strongly weathered, low fertility soils at low (site GIG), mid (site P12), and high rainfall (site SC), and one forest on high-fertility soils paired with the infertile forest at mid-rainfall (site P13). This design was used to help disentangle effects of mean annual precipitation (MAP) and soil fertility on soil responses to seasonal and experimental drying. The four forests included here were: a forest at 2350 mm MAP on strongly weathered, infertile soil on the Gigante Peninsula (GIG), two paired forests at 2600 mm MAP on the Buena Vista Peninsula, one with strongly weathered infertile soil (Plot 12 [P12]), and one with less weathered fertile soil (Plot 13 [P13]), and a forest at 3421 mm MAP on strongly weathered infertile soil on the Caribbean coast in the San Lorenzo forest at Sherman Crane (SC). Root samples were collected in 10-cm depth intervals up to 1.2 meters from 8 plots per site (totaling 32 plots) during late 2017 through 2018 when soils were wet (from the late wet season to the transition to the dry season, as described in Dietterich et al., 2022; Cusack et al., 2023b).

Root Collection: Root biomass was sampled to a depth of 1.2 meters using a 5-cm diameter hand auger. This sampling was performed in conjunction with the installation of minirhizotron tubes at a 45° angle to the soil surface (Norby et al., 2004). Due to the angled sampling, cores were collected in 14.1 cm length increments to ensure true vertical depths were in 10-cm intervals. One hole in each 10 x 10 meter plot was sampled, with plots spaced more than 10 meters apart within each forest (n = 8 per site). Samples were stored in plastic bags at 4°C and processed within a year of collection. Soil collection occurred in September 2017 (P12), December 2017 (P13), February 2018 (SC), and October 2018 (GIG), corresponding to the late wet season for P12, P13, and GIG, and the transition to the dry season in SC (Paton, 2023a, b). In total, 384 samples were collected across sites and depths. Additional root samples for assessing AMF colonization were collected from each plot using a 3.81 cm diameter constant volume corer, taking sequential cores from 0 – 10 cm and 10 – 20 cm depths at three locations per plot. AMF samples were collected in September 2018 (P12, P13, SC) and December 2018 (GIG) during the wet season. Fine roots were separated from soil, stored in plastic cassettes in tap water at 4°C until staining, and then analyzed for colonization counts.

Root Processing: Wet weights of all field samples were measured. Subsamples of 3 – 4 grams of root-free, fresh soil were oven-dried at 105°C until a constant weight was reached to determine soil moisture content and dry weight for each depth increment. Fresh soil was rinsed through a 0.25 mm sieve to remove soil from roots, which were then cleaned manually using paint brushes and water. Roots were sorted into fine (< 2 mm in diameter) and coarse (> 2 mm in diameter) categories using a caliper. Coarse roots in the collected cores were generally no larger than 3 mm, thus representing a relatively small-diameter portion of the coarse root stock. Fine roots were further classified as live or dead through visual and mechanical assessments, with live roots identified by their turgidity and intact cortex and periderm (Freschet et al., 2021a). Live fine roots were scanned to assess morphology, then dried at 60°C until a constant weight was achieved to measure biomass. Root biomass per soil mass was calculated using dry root and dry soil mass per sample (g-biomass / kg dry soil). Cumulative root biomass to 1.2 meters depth was calculated in mg/cm² by dividing the total fine root biomass for the soil profile by the soil core surface area. Standing root biomass carbon stocks were also calculated (mg C/cm²).

Root Morphology, Chemistry, and AMF Colonization: Live fine root samples were scanned at 800 dpi using a 9800XL plus-Microtek-TMA 1600 II scanner. The images were analyzed with WinRHIZO software to determine specific root length (SRL), specific root area (SRA), root tissue density (RTD), and mean root diameter. SRL (cm * mg⁻¹) represents root length per dry mass; SRA (cm² * mg⁻¹) represents root surface area per dry mass; and RTD (g * cm⁻³) represents root dry mass per volume. After drying, live root tissues were finely ground for elemental C and N analysis using a Carlo-Erba NA1500 at the Environmental Stable Isotope Laboratory at Duke University. Root chemistry was analyzed at various depths from 4 – 5 plots per site, depending on tissue availability. To calculate standing fine root carbon stocks, we multiplied the mg-biomass by the site-average fine root %C. The %C for fine roots was averaged across depths to obtain a profile average with its mean and SE reported in Table 2. Measurements were also extrapolated to Mg C/ha for comparison with other studies.
AMF colonization: roots were cleared and stained following modified protocols for tropical roots (Giovannetti & Mosse, 1980; Koske & Gemma, 1989; INVAM, 2023). Roots were cleared in 10% KOH at ~60°C for ~7 days, bleached in ~3% H2O2 at room temperature for 30 – 60 minutes, and then rinsed, acidified in 1% HCl, stained with 0.05% trypan blue in a glycerol: deionized water: 1% HCl solution at ~60°C for 30 – 60 minutes, and finally rinsed and stored in tap water at 4°C until scoring. AMF colonization was estimated as the percentage of root length containing AMF structures using the gridline-intersect method, with colonization calculated as the proportion of scorable intersections where AMF structures were observed for each plot and depth.

NMR data: A subset of dried and ground root samples (n = 6 per site) from 0 – 10 cm depth was analyzed for organic chemistry using composite pulse multi-cross polarization 13C NMR experiments on a 300 MHz Bruker Avance III NMR spectrometer at Baylor University. The pulse program included eleven contact pulses of 1.1 ms, a proton repolarization time of 0.8 s, and the sample rotor operated at a magic angle spinning frequency of 12 kHz. Spectra were analyzed for seven carbon functional groups: alkyl, N-alkyl, O-alkyl, di-O-alkyl, aromatic, phenolic, and amide+carboxyl (Min et al., 2015; Li et al., 2015). Tissue quality was assessed by calculating the lignin/N ratio, using the lignin content of roots as 26.9% of root C (Baldock et al., 2004) and the root C/N ratio.
